ops.old: By 2024, over 480 ACOs were participating in MSSP, covering more than 11 million Medicare beneficiaries.
ops.new: In 2024, 480 ACOs were participating in MSSP, covering 10.8 million Medicare beneficiaries.
ops.claim: By 2024 over 480 ACOs covering more than 11 million beneficiaries
ops.sources: CMS press release 2024-01-29 'Participation Continues to Grow in CMS' Accountable Care Organization Initiatives in 2024' and 2024 Shared Savings Program Fast Facts: 480 ACOs, 10.8 million beneficiaries
ops.note: Beneficiary count overstated; corrected to CMS figure.

ops.old: For performance year 2022, MSSP ACOs collectively generated $2.0 billion in gross savings relative to benchmarks, and $1.8 billion in net savings after shared savings payments to ACOs. Approximately 60% of MSSP ACOs earned shared savings payments.
ops.new: For performance year 2022, MSSP ACOs collectively generated about $4.3 billion in gross savings relative to benchmarks, earned a then-record $2.5 billion in shared savings payments, and produced $1.8 billion in net savings to Medicare. Of the 482 participating ACOs, 63% earned shared savings payments.
ops.sources: CMS PY2022 Shared Savings Program results (Aug 2023): $1.8B net savings, $2.5B shared savings payments, 63% of ACOs earned payments; NAACOS 'Highlights of the MSSP Results: 2022 Edition' ($4.3B gross, 482 ACOs)
ops.note: Gross figure was arithmetically impossible ($2.0B gross cannot leave $1.8B net after $2.5B of payments).

ops.old: A 2020 analysis by McWilliams and colleagues published in the New England Journal of Medicine found that new MSSP ACOs achieved minimal savings in their first 3 years, with meaningful savings concentrated in ACOs that had prior experience in risk-based contracting — particularly those who had previously participated in managed care or commercial ACO programs. Inexperienced organizations entering MSSP largely for the shared savings upside, without the care management infrastructure to generate real efficiency, produced little to no Medicare savings.
ops.new: A 2018 analysis by McWilliams and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine ("Medicare Spending after 3 Years of the Medicare Shared Savings Program") found that savings grew with length of participation and were concentrated in physician-group ACOs, which by 2015 saved Medicare a net $256 million after bonuses; in hospital-integrated ACOs, shared-savings payments offset the spending reductions, leaving no net savings.
ops.claim: 2020 McWilliams NEJM: new ACOs minimal savings; savings concentrated in ACOs with prior risk-contracting experience
ops.sources: McWilliams JM, Hatfield LA, Landon BE, Hamed P, Chernew ME. Medicare spending after 3 years of the Medicare Shared Savings Program. N Engl J Med 2018;379:1139-49 (AJMC and HealthExec coverage: physician-group ACOs net $256.4M in 2015; hospital-integrated ACOs no net savings)
ops.note: Wrong year and wrong finding; replaced with the study's actual result.

ops.old: The CMS evaluation found that Pioneer ACOs generated $385 million in gross savings over 3 years from 2012 to 2015, with average per-beneficiary savings of approximately $300.
ops.new: CMS's Office of the Actuary certified that Pioneer ACOs generated more than $384 million in savings over their first two performance years (2012 and 2013) — about $300 per participating beneficiary per year — making Pioneer the first CMMI model to meet the statutory criteria for expansion.
ops.claim: Pioneer ACOs $385M gross savings over 3 years 2012-2015, ~$300 per beneficiary
ops.sources: HHS press release 2015-05-04 'Affordable Care Act payment model saves more than $384 million in two years, meets criteria for first-ever expansion' ($279.7M PY1, $104.5M PY2; ~$300 per beneficiary per year)
ops.note: Period was two years, not three.

ops.old: However, 13 of the original 32 Pioneer ACOs dropped out of the model before its conclusion,
ops.new: However, 13 of the original 32 Pioneer ACOs left after the first year alone, and fewer than ten were still participating when the model concluded at the end of 2016,
ops.claim: 13 of 32 Pioneer ACOs dropped out before conclusion
ops.sources: CMS Pioneer ACO Model page / Abt Associates Pioneer evaluation: 32 ACOs in 2012, 13 left after PY1; model concluded 2016-12-31 with 8-9 ACOs (KFF Evidence Link FAQ: 24 of 32 withdrew)
ops.note: 13 left after year 1 (real), but 'before its conclusion' understated attrition (23 of 32 left).

ops.old: The 2021 evaluation found that NextGen ACOs generated approximately $406 million in net savings to Medicare across the model's life, representing roughly a 1.7% reduction in per-beneficiary spending. This is a meaningful but modest result for organizations operating at the leading edge of ACO capability,
ops.new: NORC's sixth and final evaluation found that NextGen ACOs reduced gross Medicare spending by about 2% (roughly $270 per beneficiary per year, about $1.7 billion in total) — but after Medicare's shared-savings and other payments to the ACOs, net Medicare spending rose slightly, by about $97 million. That is a sobering result for organizations operating at the leading edge of ACO capability,
ops.claim: 2021 evaluation: NextGen ACOs ~$406M net savings, 1.7% reduction
ops.sources: NORC at the University of Chicago, Next Generation ACO Model Sixth (Final) Evaluation Report (CMS Innovation Center data and reports): gross savings ~$1.7B (~2%), net spending increase ~$96.7M ($56 per beneficiary per year)
ops.note: Model produced no net savings; text claimed $406M net savings.

ops.old: The CMMI director at the time, Seema Verma, argued that one-sided MSSP ACOs — which faced no penalty if spending exceeded their benchmark — were providing free money to organizations with favorable benchmarks rather than incentivizing real care transformation.
ops.new: CMS Administrator Seema Verma argued in 2018 that one-sided "upside-only" MSSP ACOs — which faced no penalty if spending exceeded their benchmark, and made up 82% of ACOs that year — were actually increasing Medicare spending rather than driving real care transformation.
ops.claim: 'The CMMI director at the time, Seema Verma' argued one-sided ACOs were 'free money'
ops.sources: CMS press release 2018-08-09 'CMS proposes Pathways to Success'; Verma remarks at AHA Annual Membership Meeting 2018-05-07 (HCInnovation: 'Verma criticizes upside-only ACOs'; 460 of 561 ACOs upside-only)
ops.note: Verma was CMS Administrator, not CMMI director; paraphrase replaced with her documented claim.

ops.old: A 2023 analysis by Colla and colleagues drawing on MSSP data and ACO survey data found that the strongest predictors of sustained savings include the following.
ops.new: Studies of MSSP results and national ACO surveys point to a recurring set of characteristics associated with sustained savings.
ops.claim: 2023 analysis by Colla and colleagues identified strongest predictors of savings
ops.sources: Searched PubMed/Health Affairs/NSACO publications for a 2023 Colla et al. predictors-of-savings analysis; none found

ops.old: Multiple studies have found that MSSP ACO beneficiaries show better performance on preventive care measures, lower rates of avoidable hospitalizations, and better chronic disease management compared to matched fee-for-service controls. A 2018 study in Health Affairs by McWilliams and colleagues found that MSSP ACOs achieved greater reductions in potentially avoidable hospitalizations than non-ACO FFS, with an estimated 7% reduction in hospital admissions for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions — a meaningful improvement in care quality that also has cost implications.
ops.new: Multiple studies have found that MSSP ACO beneficiaries show better performance on preventive care and chronic disease process measures compared to matched fee-for-service controls. Avoidable admissions are a different story: a December 2017 Health Affairs study by McWilliams and colleagues found that early MSSP savings were not driven by fewer hospitalizations for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions — admissions for COPD or asthma fell, but those for heart failure and for cardiovascular disease or diabetes rose — so the savings came mostly from elsewhere.
ops.claim: 2018 Health Affairs McWilliams study: 7% reduction in ACSC admissions in MSSP ACOs
ops.sources: McWilliams JM et al., 'Medicare ACO Program Savings Not Tied To Preventable Hospitalizations Or Concentrated Among High-Risk Patients', Health Affairs 2017;36(12) doi:10.1377/hlthaff.2017.0814
ops.note: The real study found the opposite of the claimed result.

ops.old: The report acknowledged that despite more than $10 billion invested in testing alternative payment models since 2010, only a handful of models had generated statistically significant net savings to Medicare.
ops.new: The white paper acknowledged that of the more than 50 models the Innovation Center had launched since 2010, only six had generated statistically significant savings to Medicare, and only four had met the requirements to be expanded in duration and scope.
ops.claim: CMMI 2021 refresh: 'despite more than $10 billion invested ... only a handful' saved
ops.sources: CMS Innovation Center, 'Innovation Center Strategy Refresh' white paper (Oct 2021), cms.gov/priorities/innovation/strategic-direction-whitepaper; McDermott+ summary 10.25.21
ops.note: The $10B figure is not in the white paper; replaced with its actual 6-of-50+ finding.

ops.sources: CMS MSSP fast facts via RevCycleIntelligence: 561 (2018), 487 (2019), 517 (2020), 477 (2021)
